title: Prototype the Whole Service
editorial_note: Opening revised to lead with the lesson itself. Remaining dialogue is an automated editorial draft; review spoken wording and meaning before final publication.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Prototype the Whole Service.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Service prototypes rehearse the combined experience of people, policy, environment, technology, and communications. They may use role-play, concierge delivery, walkthroughs, mock artefacts, simulations, or small pilots. Their goal is to learn how the whole service behaves before expensive commitment.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Prototype the riskiest service assumptions, including handoffs and exceptions. Observe both customer and staff experience. A service is ready only when the promise, operations, and recovery paths can work together.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Choose fidelity for the service risk
turns.text: What changes when we look at choose fidelity for the service risk?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Service-prototype fidelity has several dimensions: visual representation, behavioural realism, data realism, role realism, policy authority, environmental conditions, and operational load. Raising all of them at once is expensive and can create false confidence.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team should make only the dimensions needed for the current decision realistic and state clearly what remains simulated.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Findings determine the next representation. If the state model fails, revise and rehearse it. If supplier acknowledgement is uncertain, run a technical spike. If capacity is the risk, simulate realistic volume.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: If people understand the process but live outcomes remain uncertain, move to a limited pilot with eligibility boundaries, monitoring, rollback, and pre-agreed stop conditions. Progression is based on retired uncertainty, not visual polish.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: airport assistance?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A screen prototype can test booking assistance, but not whether information reaches the airline, ground handler, security, and gate staff or whether equipment and staff are available during disruption. Role-play in the physical environment with timed handoffs may reveal the decisive failure before any software is built.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at prototype orchestration and failure?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Create a scenario that crosses channels and roles. Represent customer actions, staff decisions, messages, records, queues, policy, and time. A paper form, role-play, mocked notification, live spreadsheet, and simulated call can together reveal more than a polished front-end prototype.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Test the promise under realistic load and exception. Does information follow the person? Can staff recognise state and act? Does capacity match demand? What happens when a supplier, system, or person is unavailable? Include recovery and escalation rather than ending at the successful handoff.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Measure both sides: customer progress, understanding, effort, and dignity; staff workload, error, authority, and coordination. Record which elements were simulated and what requires a live pilot. Service prototyping reduces operational and policy risk before scale, not just usability risk.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at prototype the risky relationships?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: He stages a role-play with realistic messages, staff scripts, simulated data latency, a manual eligibility check, and failure injection. Participants encounter a disappearing slot and conflicting confirmation while team members operate the backstage process. The prototype records waiting, handoffs, workload, misunderstanding, and recovery, not only task completion.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Fidelity follows uncertainty. Paper and role-play are enough for workflow and responsibility; coded integration may be needed for timing or data behavior. Safety boundaries prevent a prototype from being mistaken for live clinical service. Findings update the blueprint, operating procedure, product design, and measurement plan together.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Whole-service prototyping reduces the risk of shipping a polished interface attached to an unworkable operation.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The cheapest prototype is often a rehearsal of policy and people, not a high-fidelity interface. Choose the representation that answers the decision at risk.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose a service prototype that tests the riskiest system behaviour. Role-play can reveal handoff and conversation issues; a concierge approach can test demand and manual operations; a simulated environment can test staff workflows; a limited pilot can test capacity, policy, and real customer expectations.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Represent the parts necessary for valid learning, including communications, waiting, data, authority, and recovery—not only the digital screen.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Observe both sides of the service. Ask what the customer understands and does, what staff need to know and decide, how long work takes, what breaks under variation, and where responsibility becomes unclear. Define safety limits and stop conditions before a live pilot.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A prototype that delights a customer while exhausting staff or relying on unsustainable manual work has revealed a problem, not validated a service.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Screen-only prototype: the UI is tested without the people, policy, or operations needed to keep its promise. Manual magic: concierge effort is treated as proof that automation or scale will work. No exception rehearsal: normal flow succeeds but recovery has never been tested. Customer-only evaluation: staff burden, capacity, and operational errors remain invisible.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A new appointment interface is tested successfully. On launch, staff lack training, rooms are unavailable, and cancellation policy conflicts with the on-screen promise. The screen was prototyped; the service was not.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Co-creation builds a shared service model. Whole-service prototyping tests it. Module 11 focuses on prototypes and evaluation across product work.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Design a low-cost rehearsal for a service change without building software. What would it reveal about people, policy, or handoffs?
